P1.evidence: Application referenced but not read back: 'Look, I saw your application. But yeah, let's get into more details...' The frame that followed carried two of the four parts — where you are and what you have tried — but not where you want to go or what you need, so P1b is partial. Agreement was sought and given ('Cool.' / 'Yeah, that sounds good'). The open question ran. Worth crediting separately: at 00:22:18 the rep set a genuine mid-call frame that put the decision explicitly on the table — 'Let me share with you what I'm thinking, what's going on, and how I think we could help you out, and you decide whether you want to move forward with this or not' — which is the framing move missing from every other call in this batch, just delivered forty minutes late.

P2.evidence: The strongest baseline in the batch, six clean hits. Work was not just asked but interrogated — 'Would you mind sharing what you're doing currently for work?' then 'when you say that the job is demanding, you mean like long hours or in what way' — and the rep then challenged the prospect's own minimisation of it: 'In your opinion, that's not demanding? That's freaking 10 hours of really high-pressure environment work and then you don't switch off.' Injuries and chronic pain asked with the duration and mechanism probe: 'That pain, do you think it's a result of years of neglecting something, or it happened just like rapidly?' plus a scan for hips and knees. Training week asked and the gap named: 'So nothing really structured?' Diet walked through properly, including satiety, eating out and a favourite dish. Sleep asked twice and in unusual depth — rested on waking, bedtime, wake time, and sleep latency ('when you lay down, is it more of like two minutes and I'm gone?'). Energy pursued all the way to the narcolepsy and Adderall disclosure. What is missing is physical: no height, no weight, no body composition, and age only because the prospect volunteered it. For a client whose goal includes regaining muscle mass there is no starting measurement of any kind.

P3.evidence: Contains the single best-executed moment in the batch. The can't-do-it question ran in its most effective form and was pursued across three turns: 'When was the last time you played tennis?' / 'Do you miss it?' / 'Would it be a crazy idea if you could actually do that and play a tournament?' — which moved the prospect from 'I don't want to ever play a tennis tournament or probably even a match again in my life' to 'Like, hell yeah, that'd be awesome. I would love to do that.' The reflect-back also landed cleanly: 'it's not something that you want to lose weight... it's more of getting this upper back in check... and just basically feeling strong, more mobile in your body for the upcoming years,' confirmed with 'That's it. I just want to not be in pain and I want to feel strong.' Where it stops short is the social layer. Nobody asked who else this impacts. The prospect is married and his wife appears in this transcript only as someone who cooks; no children were established either way. Longevity landed but as the rep's frame rather than the prospect's, and the bridge question was never asked in any form.

P4.evidence: Past attempts were asked in the opener and produced an exhaustive list — PT, acupuncture, massage, yoga, nerve blockers, muscle relaxers — with the outcome stated plainly and probed by the rep for cause. The gap got named by the prospect in exactly the terms the phase wants: 'No, really lacking structure', 'I don't really know what I'm trying to accomplish', and the decisive one, 'the only thing I really haven't done is a regimented strength and mobility program, right? All the therapies I've tried have been like passive in a way.' That sentence sold the programme. But the prospect supplied it rather than being asked for it, and the closing move — 'the information isn't the problem, why can't you stick to it on your own' — never ran, even though the prospect had teed it up perfectly with 'it's not like I don't know what to do in the gym.'

P5.evidence: The only consequence work was delivered as an anecdote rather than a question: the rep's story about a friend's father, around 65, who 'didn't take care of himself' and now 'even with his technique, he's not able to compete.' That is a two-year projection told at the prospect instead of drawn out of him, and it is the entire phase. No settle question, no 'why not', no line in the sand. This is the recurring structural weakness across every call in this batch — P5 has not run properly once — and here it did not cost the deal only because the prospect arrived pre-motivated by four years of pain.

P6.evidence: The check ran as a general temperature read rather than the scripted belief question — 'How do you feel about everything that I just went through? Any thoughts on that? Any questions?' — answered 'No, I'm just super excited to do it.' The all-in question was never asked. P6c nonetheless scores a hit: the rep did have an unambiguous yes before going to price, and the prospect volunteered it repeatedly and without prompting — 'I'm so ready for it', 'Those things are important to me, and I need to find a way to make them part of my life', and 'I feel excited about this, and I'm fully ready to just dive in and do it and not quit.' There was no hesitation to return to Phase 5 for.

P11.evidence: The most complete P11 in the batch. Payment link pasted into the Zoom chat immediately after the yes, and the downstream sequence confirmed live — the prospect reported three emails and identified each, which is the post-payment flow. Onboarding booked for Monday 3:15pm Eastern from Trevor's calendar with four slots offered. The agreement email was confirmed as arrived and identified by the prospect, but he was never asked to sign it on the call, so P11c is partial. Step four was covered fully and better than elsewhere: the onboarding form to complete before the Trevor session and the Primal University community invitation were both named and explained. Deduction only that the rep never verbally confirmed funds cleared, which he did do on the Chris Wiley call.

objection_plays.detail: No think-about-it trigger. The prospect said 'let's do it' within seconds of the price being named.
No spouse-consult trigger, despite the prospect being married. He never raised his wife as part of the decision.

No money objection of any kind — the only $6,000 close in this batch with zero price resistance, no discount request and no payment plan asked for or offered. Notable given the rep improvised off-book instalment structures on four other calls in the same batch.
No timing objection. The prospect had already started kettlebells on his own two weeks earlier and pushed toward starting immediately.

No fear or doubt trigger about the programme. The nearest thing was learned helplessness about his back — 'can I really commit to doing this five days a week, when I don't know if it's helping?' — which surfaced in P4 as history rather than as a live objection, and the rep converted it into the passive-versus-active therapy frame.

Continuity question about the handoff: 'What about you? What's your involvement from here on out?' No scripted play exists, and the rep handled it correctly by simply telling the truth — 'I'm only in the front-end. You're going to be working only with Trevor' — then explaining that Trevor deliberately structured the business around coaching rather than selling. The prospect finished the argument himself. Worth capturing as a reusable answer; the same question in a more suspicious form ('Is Trevor an AI-generated person?') appears elsewhere in this batch.

SCRIPT GAP — the clinical gate, and the most serious instance of it in this batch alongside Steve Dawson. The prospect disclosed four to five years of progressively worsening spinal pain, disc desiccation on imaging, a prior herniated disc, a history of nerve blockers and muscle relaxers, and diagnosed narcolepsy on daily Adderall. The playbook contains no move requiring clearance before purchase, so none was sought. Worse, the absence of a scripted boundary let the rep fill the space with a causal explanation of his own — 'it sounds to me that it is a result of this demanding work... the stress is just piling up' — and then encourage a return to the tennis serve, the movement that herniated the disc. A mandatory clearance question in P2d would have cost this call nothing; the prospect was already sold.

notes: The best-run call in the batch on process and the second most exposed on risk. Baseline was excellent, the tennis question in P3 is a training clip, P11 was completed properly, and the price held at $6,000 with no plan and no resistance. Two things to fix, neither of which would have threatened the sale: P5 still has not run once across this rep's calls, and a prospect with disc desiccation, a prior herniation and daily Adderall was closed on ballistic loading with no clearance question and an off-the-cuff causal theory about his spine. Coach the boundary line — 'that is a question for your doctor' — and add a hard clearance gate before any close involving a disclosed spinal condition.
